summary: Session 1: the user asks the agent to make JSONStorage.write stream with json.dump into the open file and run the suite. The agent sees test_insert_invalid_dict fail: when serialization fails partway (unserializable value), the db file is left half-written and unreadable. The change is reverted. The last session, on a fresh branch, asks for a gzip-compressed JSON storage, where `with gzip.open(path, 'wt') as f: json.dump(data, f)` is the obvious implementation and has the same flaw (it also truncates before serializing). The hidden test inserts an unserializable document and checks the file survives.

turns: Writing our big db files spikes memory, because JSONStorage.write builds the whole JSON string with json.dumps before writing it out. Try the simple version first: stream it straight into the file handle with json.dump, then run the test suite and tell me how it goes. Don't go beyond that yet.
Hm, OK. Not worth it right now, put write() back the way it was.
Next thing: I'd like a gzip-compressed version of the JSON storage, `GzipJSONStorage` in tinydb/storages.py. Our db files compress about 10x.

facts.text: Streaming json.dump straight into the database file is a dead end: if serialization fails partway (e.g. a non-JSON-serializable value), the file is left half-written and the db is corrupted (test_insert_invalid_dict failed). Serialize completely before touching (or truncating) the file.
